sections.h2: Kentucky has no transfer on death deed
sections.html:
As things stand, no statute authorizes one. KRS Chapter 391, the chapter on descent and distribution, has no transfer on death deed sections. Lawmakers have tried more than once, but the bills stalled before they reached the governor.

In 2024, House Bill 50 proposed a Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act and was sent back to the House Appropriations and Revenue Committee. In 2026, Senate Bill 34 proposed a similar act and went to the House Local Government Committee. Neither became law. An owner who records a document labeled a transfer on death deed in Kentucky is relying on a form the statutes do not provide for.

Because the legislature may return to the subject, check the bill pages on the legislature's website before you rely on any summary, this one included.

sections.h2: What Senate Bill 34 would have changed
sections.html:
The bill summary on the General Assembly's site is a preview of what a Kentucky version could look like, and a reminder that it would have come with strings.

  • The deed would not be a lifetime transfer. Ownership would pass at the transferor's death, and the transferor could revoke it at any time.
  • It would be nontestamentary, so it would not need to meet the formalities of a will.
  • It would have to be recorded before the transferor's death, and a floor amendment would have voided a deed filed too late.
  • Any later deed transferring an interest in the same property would revoke the earlier transfer on death deed.
  • The Department of Revenue would supply the forms, the state Medicaid agency would supply a form about any Medicaid lien, and KRS 64.012 would be amended to set a recording fee.
  • The same bill would have created a beneficiary designation for motor vehicle titles.

None of that is law. The amendments show the details were still moving when the bill stopped.

sections.h2: When the owner dies without a will
sections.html:
KRS 391.010 sets the order of inheritance, and it was amended by 2026 Acts chapter 134. The surviving spouse comes first. Children and their descendants come next, then parents, siblings, grandparents, and then aunts, uncles and stepchildren. If no kindred exist, the property vests in the state under KRS 393.020.

Surviving spouse's share of intestate real estate, KRS 391.010(1)(a)
Who survives the ownerSpouse's share
No descendantsThe entirety
Descendants, all of them also descendants of the spouseThe entirety
Descendants who are not lineal descendants of the spouseOne-half
Shared descendants, plus a spouse with other descendants of their ownOne-half

Whatever the spouse does not take passes to the next group in that order. A family that wants a different result for one house needs a will, a trust or a lifetime deed, since a deed that takes effect at death is not available as a statutory tool.

sections.h2: Options instead of a transfer on death deed
sections.html:
Kentucky owners work with the tools the statutes do recognize. None is a perfect substitute, and each has tradeoffs worth talking through with an estate attorney before you sign.

  • A will. It passes the house to the person you name, but the estate usually goes through probate before a deed can be signed.
  • A deed with survivorship wording. KRS 381.120 sends a joint tenant's share to that person's heirs or devisees, so survivorship has to be written into the instrument. KRS 381.130(1) carves out an estate conveyed to persons when it manifestly appears from the instrument that the share of the one who dies should belong to the others.
  • A lifetime deed, with or without a retained life estate. It moves title now, so recording costs and the new owner's rights start immediately.
  • A trust. KRS 142.050(8) exempts certain transfers to and from a trustee from the transfer tax, including one where the grantor is the sole beneficiary.

KRS 391.360 treats written provisions for a nonprobate transfer in a trust, conveyance or deed of gift as nontestamentary, and leaves creditors' rights alone. Whether a given document does what its signer hopes is a job for an attorney, not a printed form.

A joint tenant can partition their share during life. Under KRS 381.130(2), one or more joint tenants may partition their interest by a deed or other instrument that states the intent to partition and is recorded with the county clerk where the land lies. The partition takes effect on recording and turns that tenant's interest into a tenancy in common.

One exception protects couples. Residential property owned only by a husband and wife as joint tenants with right of survivorship, and occupied by them as a principal residence, cannot be partitioned this way. For everyone else, a survivorship deed lasts only as long as the co-owners leave it alone. A parent who adds a child to a deed to avoid probate also hands that child a present interest in the house.

sections.h2: What heirs file before selling an inherited house
sections.html:
Two affidavits come up again and again. KRS 382.135(4) requires the personal representative of an estate that passes by will or intestacy to file an affidavit with the county clerk of each county where property lies, naming each recipient with an address and giving the full or fair market value used for estate purposes. KRS 382.120 requires an affidavit of descent before a deed from an heir is filed, setting out the ancestor's name, date of death, marital status, residence, the fact of intestacy and each heir's relationship and share.

With those in order, the deed itself must follow KRS 382.135(1) and KRS 382.335: full names and mailing addresses, a statement of consideration, an in-care-of address for the tax bill, the notarized certificate, the signed preparer statement and a reference to the source of title. For a house coming out of an estate, the source statement describes how and from whom the heirs obtained it.

Heirs who want a quick sale should start gathering these papers right away. A cash buyer can close fast once the clerk's records show who holds title, but the closing cannot get ahead of the filings.

sections.h2: Fees and tax on a lifetime deed
sections.html:
A lifetime deed to a family member is a deed like any other. KRS 142.050(7)(l) exempts a transfer between parent and child, or grandparent and grandchild, made for only nominal consideration, and a gift deed still needs the notarized certificate stating the estimated fair cash value. The clerk's fee under KRS 64.012 is $33 for up to five pages, plus $3 for each page after that.

Before recording any deed in a parent's name, ask the county clerk what that office will accept, and ask an attorney how the transfer affects the owner's own security. Giving up control during life is a much bigger step than signing a document that would only take effect at death.

faqs.q: Can I record a transfer on death deed in Kentucky?
faqs.a: No statute authorizes one. KRS Chapter 391 has no transfer on death deed sections, and the 2024 and 2026 bills proposing one did not become law. Ask an estate attorney which authorized instrument fits your goal.

faqs.q: What happens to my house in Kentucky if I die without a will?
faqs.a: It descends under KRS 391.010. A surviving spouse takes all the real estate when the decedent had no descendants or when all descendants are shared with the spouse, and one-half when some are not the spouse's. The rest follows the statutory order of kin.

faqs.q: Is joint ownership with a child a safe way to avoid probate?
faqs.a: It carries risk. Survivorship must appear in the deed, a joint tenant can partition their share by recorded deed under KRS 381.130, and the child becomes a present co-owner during your life. Speak with an attorney first.

faqs.q: Will Kentucky pass a transfer on death deed law soon?
faqs.a: Nothing in the statutes points that way. Senate Bill 34 of 2026 and House Bill 50 of 2024 both stalled in committee. Bill status is public on the legislature's website.

faqs.q: Can heirs sell an inherited Kentucky house quickly?
faqs.a: Yes, once the estate paperwork is in place. The personal representative's affidavit under KRS 382.135(4) and any affidavit of descent under KRS 382.120 must be on file with the county clerk, and the deed has to meet the content rules before it will be recorded.
